title: Morocco
hookLine: the night Passover ends, Moroccan Jewish homes open their doors to neighbors for Mimouna

cards: Passover ends at nightfall. For a week, no bread in the house. And in Moroccan Jewish homes, almost as the last blessing is said, the kitchen comes alive.
Flour comes out. Thin pancakes go into the pan, eaten warm with butter and honey. The table fills with sweets, fresh milk, green stalks of wheat.
The front door stays open, and the neighbors come in, Jewish and not. Today's word is the name of that night.

teach.h: A NAME NOBODY IS SURE OF.
teach.b: Mimouna. Nobody is quite sure where the name comes from. Some connect it to Maimon, the father of Maimonides, said to have died around this time of year.
Others hear in it the Hebrew emunah, faith, or an Arabic word for good fortune. The custom is clearer than the name.
On Mimouna night, families set a table like a wish for the year ahead: honey for sweetness, milk for plenty, wheat for a good harvest, sometimes a fish for blessing.
Guests walk from house to house, greeting each other with a Judeo-Arabic blessing for success and good luck.
Then there are the neighbors. In Morocco, tradition says, Muslim neighbors would bring flour, butter and milk to Jewish homes as Passover ended, since their own kitchens had none, and stay to eat.
The party became a meeting place. When Moroccan Jews moved to Israel, they brought Mimouna with them, and the open door became an open park, with picnics that welcome whoever comes.
The Torah gives a simple rule that this night acts out: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Mimouna turns it into flour, pancakes and an unlocked door. Look back at this week, too.
A Sanhedrin called by Napoleon. Reform beginning. Hirsch joining Torah with the world.
Frankel's middle path. The Mortaras' terrible night. The Targum in Yemen.
And now a door in Morocco, wide open after Passover.

how: On the night Passover ends, Moroccan Jewish families set a table with mufleta pancakes, honey, milk and greenery, visit from house to house with blessings, and in Israel the next day often brings large outdoor picnics.

games.q: Passover has just ended in Morocco. your Jewish neighbors have had no flour all week. what do you bring, tradition says?
games.why: tradition says Muslim neighbors brought flour, butter and milk, then stayed to eat at the open table.

practice: Think of the people who live closest to you, and notice which ones you know by name. Choose one, and picture handing them something small and sweet, with the door staying open a minute longer than usual.

wordCard.voice: Mimouna. The Moroccan Jewish celebration on the night Passover ends, with sweet food, blessings for the year, and doors open to neighbors. Today's word.

orig.note: the name of the night after Passover; where the name comes from is still argued.

carryVoice: Your line: the front door stays open. Sweet things are better shared. Day nine hundred eighty, and a week complete.
